turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was not satisfied with his answers and that he had yet to convince her of his suitability as a husband for her daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was afraid he had not been entirely truthful with Lady Bracknell, and that he wished to make amends by telling the truth, even if it seemed foolish or unsuitable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was shocked, yet not entirely surprised, by his admission of dishonesty, and that his candor, while commendable, hardly redeemed his initial deceit.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked if he might be allowed to explain the reasons behind his initial dishonesty, hoping that a full understanding of the circumstances might help to alleviate Lady Bracknell's concerns.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack to explain these circumstances, but warned him that she would not tolerate any further prevarication or dishonesty.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had grown up in a poor family and had never had much formal education, which was why he had felt so intimidated by the prospect of marrying into a family like the Bracknells, and that his dishonesty was a desperate attempt to make a good impression.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her disapproval of Jack's upbringing and education, or rather, lack thereof, and asked how he expected to hold his own in polite society, let alone with a family like the Bracknells, where refinement and breeding were of the utmost importance.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he understood her concerns and respected the importance of refinement and breeding, but he was willing to learn and make a genuine effort to adapt to the Bracknells' way of life, especially for Gwendolen's sake.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she had had quite enough of this inquisition and that she would much rather her mother was asking her own daughter about her suitability as a wife for Jack.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell informed Jack that she would not consider his willingness to learn and adapt as a suitable replacement for breeding and refinement, which could only be acquired through birth and upbringing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was not expecting to be a member of the Bracknell family, but rather to be married to Gwendolen, and that he hoped his love for her and his desire to make her happy would be enough to outweigh any perceived shortcomings in his background.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen firmly stated that she was not about to be judged solely on her mother's standards, and that she would not be considered unsuitable just because she was marrying someone from a lower social class.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that his love for Gwendolen, while commendable, was hardly a substitute for a respectable family name and a proper education, and that his attempts to justify his own inadequacies were quite beside the point.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack expressed his concern that, if his background was to be held against him, he feared it would be impossible to meet Lady Bracknell's standards, and that he would rather not proceed with the engagement if it was to be a source of disappointment for her.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted that she would not be swayed by such sentimental notions as love and happiness, and that the suitability of her daughter's husband was of the utmost importance.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen demanded to know why her mother was being so obstinate, and why she couldn't see that her love for Jack was all that mattered.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell stated that her daughter's happiness was of little consequence if the marriage would compromise the family's social standing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he understood her concerns about social standing, but he couldn't help but think that Gwendolen's happiness was the most important thing in this situation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Jack with a disapproving gaze, telling him that his notion of happiness was far too simplistic and naive.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was not trying to be simplistic, but rather, he genuinely believed that Gwendolen's happiness was what truly mattered in this situation.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
